yt_titulo: Why Isn't the Netherlands Underwater?
yt_descricao:
A quarter of the Netherlands sits below sea level. So why isn't it underwater?

In 1953 a North Sea storm surge broke through the dikes: 1,836 people died and more than 1,300 km² flooded. The answer was the Delta Works, 13 dams and storm barriers built from 1958 to 1997, ending with the Maeslantkering, two giant gates that close on their own when the sea rises. Today the heart of the country is built to survive a storm expected once in 10,000 years.

yt_titulo: A Fifth of the World's Oil Goes Through This Gap
yt_descricao:
One fifth of the world's oil sails through one channel, and in 2026 it almost stopped.

The Strait of Hormuz is about 33 km wide at its narrowest, with two shipping lanes about 3 km wide each. In 2024 about 20 million barrels of oil a day passed through it, roughly a fifth of world use. Saudi and UAE bypass pipelines have only a few million barrels a day of spare room, so when traffic collapsed in 2026, Brent crude passed $100 a barrel.

yt_descricao:
There's a cathedral 50 meters under Tokyo, and nobody prays there.

The Metropolitan Area Outer Underground Discharge Channel (G-Cans) protects Greater Tokyo from floods: when rivers overflow, water drops into five giant silos, runs through 6.4 km of tunnels into a 177 m long tank held up by 59 pillars, and is pumped into the Edo River at up to 200 tonnes per second. Built from 1992 to 2006.

yt_titulo: Ships Climb a Lake 26 Meters Above the Sea
yt_descricao:
In Panama, ships climb a staircase of water to cross a continent.

The Panama Canal is 82 km long and its middle, Gatun Lake, sits 26 m above the sea. Three locks lift every ship up and three more lower it on the other side, and each crossing sends about 200 million liters of fresh water into the ocean. In 2023 the rain didn't come: by December only 22 ships a day could cross instead of 36.

yt_titulo: Italy Approved This Bridge, Then Blocked It
yt_descricao:
Italy approved the world's longest suspension bridge. Then its own auditors blocked it.

The Strait of Messina Bridge would have a 3,300 m main span, about 60% longer than today's record (Çanakkale 1915 Bridge, 2,023 m), 399 m towers, and a design for magnitude 7.8 earthquakes, for about €13.5 billion. It was approved in August 2025, refused registration by the Court of Auditors in October 2025 and restarted by a new decree in February 2026. As of October 2026, construction has not started.

yt_titulo: Venice Has a Wall You Can't See
yt_descricao:
Venice is protected by a wall you can't see.

It's called MOSE: 78 steel gates lying on the seabed across the three entrances to the Venetian lagoon (Lido, Malamocco and Chioggia). Normally they're full of water and out of sight. When a high tide is coming, air is pumped in, the water is pushed out and the gates rise. Construction began in 2003; on October 3, 2020 they rose for the first time and kept Venice dry. Cost: about €5.5 billion.

yt_titulo: They're Sinking 89 Giant Blocks Into the Sea

They're sinking 89 concrete blocks into the Baltic Sea, and each standard block weighs 73,500 tonnes.

Together they'll form the Fehmarnbelt Tunnel between Germany and Denmark, about 18 km long, the longest immersed tunnel on Earth. The train will cross in 7 minutes instead of 45 on the ferry, and Hamburg to Copenhagen drops from about 5 hours to about 2.5. The first block went down in May 2026, but the opening is about two years late.

The Strait of Gibraltar is deep: even its shallowest point, the Camarinal Sill, is about 280 m down. The current design runs 42 km terminal to terminal, 27.7 km under the sea, dipping to 475 m below sea level. Spain and Morocco set up study companies in 1980, and the target is now 2035 to 2040. So far the money goes to studies and seabed surveys; no tunnel boring machine has been ordered.

yt_titulo: Hong Kong Flattened Two Islands for an Airport
yt_descricao:
Hong Kong flattened two islands to build one airport.

The old airport, Kai Tak, sat in the middle of the city with one runway sticking into the harbor, and by the 1990s one in three flights was delayed. So engineers flattened Chek Lap Kok and Lam Chau and reclaimed more than 9 km² from the sea. Construction started in 1991 and the new airport opened in July 1998.

yt_titulo: Africa's Biggest Dam and the Fight Over the Nile
yt_descricao:
This is Africa's biggest hydropower dam, and the country downstream calls it an existential threat.

The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile opened in September 2025 with 5,150 MW of capacity. Its main wall is 145 m high and about 1.8 km long, and its reservoir holds 74 billion cubic meters. The Blue Nile carries about 85% of the Nile's water, and Egypt relies on the Nile for about 90% of its water. Construction began in 2011, and the countries still haven't agreed on how to share the river.
